He notes that July payroll reports over recent years have consistently surprised to the downside and have been the catalyst for significant Fed policy pivots toward rate cuts at subsequent meetings. A soft July print would reinforce expectations that the Fed is done hiking or may cut sooner, while also weighing on the US dollar's 'exceptionalism' narrative.
quote: That payroll support is really gonna be, to me, a really key piece of the jigsaw puzzle, not only when it comes to the dollar outlook, but when it comes to the Fed outlook as well. This whole broader narrative about US economic exceptionalism. What we've seen over recent years is there's been a deterioration in the US labor force data that's come out over the summer months. And we got a downside surprise that came through in the June report, of course, a month ago. So I'm intrigued to see what will happen in July, because if you think back over the past couple of years, the July report has been really, really soft. And it's been the catalyst behind this big pivot we've seen in those years, where the Fed almost immediately started cutting rates at the subsequent meeting.

headline: Iron ore price action is bearish — breakdown below 725 support and next key support at 683 with significant downside below that
reasoning: Scott describes iron ore futures as having broken down sharply through the 725 support level in renminbi terms, with the price moving like a hot knife through butter. The next key support is at 683, which held on multiple occasions last year. He notes that oscillators and moving averages are all lurching lower, pointing to further downside risk. If 683 breaks, the next level is 630, below which there is little technical support. Seasonal factors — Northern Hemisphere summer slowdown in Chinese construction activity — add to the bearish near-term outlook.
quote: You can see there, it's just had this absolute lurch lower. These are all priced in renminbi in UN. So 725 was a level that it was supported at. And after that breakdown, it just got on like a hot knife through butter. So 683 is an important level underneath. That is a support zone that held on multiple occasions back last year. So that is the area to watch when it comes to iron ore futures at the moment in China. If that holds, we could go and see a bit of retracement to squeeze back up. But right now the price action, the oscillators, the moving averages that are lurching lower, all points to downside risks. So 683 goes, 630 is the next level to watch. And beneath that, there is not a lot of technical support.

headline: RBA hike risk remains but household spending data this week is key — further softness would confirm the RBA is done
reasoning: Scott notes that while RBA Governor Bullock's speech sounded hawkish, the Q&A revealed that the housing market is cooling faster than expected. The RBA has made clear it needs to see domestic demand soften to eliminate sticky inflation, and this week's household spending data will be a crucial read on that. Scott's base case is that continued softness would build his expectation that the RBA is done, but he acknowledges the risk of at least one more hike remains.
quote: When it comes to the RBA, there's still guidance to go that there's still potential risk for a hike. But this week, we've had the big, big boppers out of the way in terms of the labor market report and inflation. This week, though, it's household spending. And this is probably underappreciated. The RBA has made it clear that one way or another, they need to see domestic demand continue to soften to kind of snuff out those domestic supply side risks there, demand side risks, sorry, that have kept inflation sticky... Continued softness there, we're just going in hands and build my expectation that the RBA is done. But you've got to admit at this point in time, there is still a chance that the RBA may be forced to go and hike at least once more.

headline: Crude prices are slumping on Iran deal hopes but Scott questions the durability of this narrative, noting the market has heard it many times before
reasoning: Scott observes that the recurring Trump-Iran nuclear deal narrative reliably drives a sharp initial reaction in oil and equity futures, but the pattern has repeated so many times that credibility is diminishing. The market's reaction function remains consistent — futures reprice sharply on headlines — but the follow-through is increasingly questioned. He uses this as context for the day's mild equity market positivity in Australia.
quote: I know deals back on the table, a nuclear deal, deal to go and open the straights completely. No strings attached, but I don't know how many times we've gone and heard the same story over and over again. It is a lot now, but the one reaction function is exactly the same time and time again. And that's where you see the futures go and repire.

headline: Joint US-Japan yen intervention is puzzling given extremely low prior volatility, with dollar-yen likely to retrace higher into US payrolls on Friday
reasoning: David Scott notes that the joint US-Japan intervention in the yen is surprising because realized volatility in dollar-yen was exceptionally low before the intervention — in the 15th percentile on a 20-day window and 0.4th percentile on a 60-day window. He questions why the US is involved and observes that the intervention sold euros through the NY Fed rather than US dollars directly. He expects the intervention to wind down soon as authorities typically operate in three-day windows, suggesting a potential dollar rebound into payrolls. He views the current dollar weakness as largely artificial, driven by the Fed rate-hike probability being priced out and yen strengthening from intervention.
quote: We've been hearing a lot from Japanese authorities in particular about warning that intervention was coming. And then the introduction of the US into the equation is really interesting. And all the reports are that it didn't go and sell US dollars. It sold euros through its New York Fed branch to go and do that. Now, as to their reason why, the Japanese authorities, the US authorities, Scott Besant was out on X earlier today talking about unruly movements and extreme volatility. But that just simply is not the case... over a 20-day window, it was in the 15th percentile. So fairly rare in the broader scheme of things over the past two decades. Over a 60-day window, it's in the 0.4th percentile, like almost unheard of levels of low volatility. So going back to your original question, it's like, why do you think that they're intervening jointly in this particular environment? It's a head scratcher.

headline: Break of symmetrical triangle in US treasury futures signals upside risk for long-end yields, which is a headwind for risk appetite
reasoning: Scott highlights a clean break of a symmetrical triangle in US long-bond futures, pointing to upside risk for 10-year and longer yields. He notes that this contract tends to trend, making the technical signal meaningful. Rising real and nominal yields in the US are historically not conducive to sustained risk appetite in equity markets, which he views as a medium-term concern for global equities.
quote: What we're seeing at the moment is that there is a clear shift going underway when it comes to the backend of the US treasury curve. So I'm talking about 10 year and out in terms of yields. And so this is a futures contract... we've seen a break of this symmetrical triangle. Now, I hear a lot of narratives day to day that people go and sprout, including for myself. But when you look at the price action itself, it is really clean and it tends to trend this contract, which means that when it goes down, it points to upside risk for yields. So when I'm looking at now, what does that mean for more broader financial markets? It suggests to me that we're gonna see real yields in the United States, nominal yields continue to go and drift higher. And that is typically not an environment that risk appetite tends to go and last well over longer periods of time.

headline: RBA August rate hike probability falling sharply on lower oil prices; Bullock speech tomorrow key event risk
reasoning: Scutt notes that the probability of an RBA hike in August has dropped from just under 50% to below 30% in just a few hours, driven by the fall in energy prices following the US-Iran de-escalation. He highlights Michelle Bullock's speech at the Annika Foundation lunch as a historically market-moving event, and speculates she may use it to set conditionality around the upcoming Q2 CPI print for whether the RBA resumes tightening.
quote: You mentioned what was going on. So late last week, it was around about just under 50% chance of a high coming through in August. As a result of what we're seeing with the energy prices over the course of the last few hours, it's now beneath 30%. So we're seeing quite a big retracting of that. Let's see what Michelle Bullock has to go say tomorrow. She's addressing the Annika Foundation lunch. And so this has been historically an event that really can be market moving when it comes to the Australian rates market and how it's perceived to see where the risks are when it comes to our interest rates moving forward.

headline: Hyperscaler CapEx trajectory is key risk for AI supply chain; Apple's relative restraint has been rewarded by markets
reasoning: Scutt highlights that Alphabet's increase in CapEx was not well received by the market, and wonders whether other hyperscalers reporting this week — Amazon, Microsoft, Meta — might follow suit. He observes that Apple, which has not aggressively ramped AI CapEx despite Siri's shortcomings, has outperformed the Mag 7 this year, suggesting the market may reward moderation. He warns that any slowdown in CapEx from hyperscalers would hurt upstream chip makers significantly.
quote: If you go and just look at some of the Mad 7 names and not so much the picks and shovels like the video, but all those who are actually hyper scalers, the one that's really set out this whole entire AI boom and revolutions and build out has been Apple. Now Siri is obviously not the best product right now, but it has been rewarded. You can see there on the chart, it is absolutely outperformed this year. And so there's probably a message there to some of these hyper scalers that, hey, it's great that you want to go and try and build up this new technology. We all know it's going to be around and probably very influential in the future. But at this point in time, there's probably nothing wrong with saying, you know what? We think there might actually go and be encased ago and slow the pace a little bit. Now that might reward the hyper scalers, but the upstream areas, the chip makers and everything else, they would really suffer the consequences of that.

headline: Brent crude 50-day moving average is key technical level to watch as Middle East conflict cools
reasoning: David Scutt notes that Brent crude is testing its 50-day moving average, which during the early stages of the conflict acted as a strong support with big bounces on each test. The 50-day moving average has since rolled over and is being tested again. If oil breaks below it, the path of least resistance is lower, which would likely extend the risk-on moves seen in Asian equities today. He views price action at that level as more informative than the headline news flow.
quote: So this is the Brent Crew daily contract. And all I've done is I've just gone and just highlighted with the red dots there, basically where we saw probes of the 50 day moving average back in the early stages of the war. And you saw that during that particular period, any test of that period, despite the headlines that were contrary to what the actual prevailing trend were, we saw big bounces. So in the near term, I think the 50 day moving average gives us some sort of sense as to where energy is moving potentially over the next couple of days. We'll now come back and we've seen that 50 day moving averages rolled over. We've seen it tested once back late last week and it bounced. Again, we're testing it again. So to me, the price action at that particular level today is going to be really informative. If we see a move back beneath it, it tells me that in the near term at least, the path of least business is lower.

headline: Fed Chair Walsh likely to stonewall on forward guidance; vote split on rate hike will be the key signal this week
reasoning: Scutt expects the Fed to keep rates unchanged but notes a roughly one-in-three chance of a hike, which in his view may be slightly underpriced. He anticipates Walsh will deflect any questions on forward guidance as he did at the last meeting. The most informative piece of data from the meeting is likely to be the vote split among FOMC members — how many voted to hike versus hold — which may provide the clearest signal about the path towards September.
quote: He'll go and talk about some of the debate that was going on within the FOMC. But when it comes to what he's going to go and deliver, he's not going to go and be committed one way or another. So unless the Fed stuns us with a rate increase, now it's not out of the realms of possibility. It's about a one-in-three chance. And potentially maybe a little bit underpriced in my opinion given some of the moves we're seeing. If we just go and get the Fed funds rate left unchanged, we're going to probably have to go and lean really heavily on the actual vote split. How many FOMC members voted to go and hike rates? How many voted to go and keep them unchanged? That might be the closest we get to any real information about what the Fed is thinking as we move towards the September meeting.

headline: CXMT's 500% IPO day gain in Shanghai is typical for Chinese listings but sustainability is uncertain
reasoning: Scutt notes that a large first-day stag profit is common for IPOs in China regardless of the sector, so CXMT's 500% debut gain is not surprising in that context. He draws a parallel to SpaceX's large initial pop in the US followed by a full reversal. CXMT is China's largest memory chip producer and the fourth largest globally, but Scutt cautions that the excitement around the AI-linked IPO does not necessarily mean gains will be sustained longer term and says investors should watch the price action closely.
quote: It's telling you that China has not gone and changed its ways regardless of what kind of company is listing. If you go back over time, it's really, really unusual to see anything but a really substantial stag profit on day one. But then you go look back and say it's not unusual to see lots of hype, lots of excitement around IPOs to deal with the AI space. Have a look at SpaceX, of course, in the United States not that long ago. It had like a massive gain in the first few days of trading. And then I learned it all. So yes, there's a lot of excitement out there. But memory chips, which is what CXMT specializes in, it's the biggest producer in China, about the fourth biggest overall globally. Doesn't necessarily mean that it's going to be sustained longer term.

headline: David Scutt says the ECB is caught between fighting inflation and mounting economic risks from energy supply disruption, and doubts rate hikes will solve the supply shock or support the euro
reasoning: Scutt characterises the ECB as being between a rock and a hard place: as a single-mandate central bank focused solely on inflation, it must tighten even as economic risks are rising from energy supply disruptions, particularly in downstream distillate products. The ECB held rates at its latest meeting but signalled the next meeting is a live event for a hike. Scutt is sceptical that rate increases will resolve a supply-side shock or meaningfully support the euro, answering no to both questions.
quote: ECB are between a rock and a hard place. So single mandate central bank inflation only uh certainly economic risks have increased by the fact that energy supply and not just crude but more so the distillers know the the downstream products is going to be a real crunch point for Europe in particular. But they can only go and fight inflation. That's what their job is at ECB. So yes, they didn't go and hike last night, but they made it pretty clear that the next meeting is a very, very live event. Uh, is the supply shock going to be solved by uh by interest rate increases? Will the euro be supported by interest rate increases? My answer to both is no.

headline: David Scutt sees US 10-year yields potentially retesting 5% as real yields approach 2023 highs and Treasury futures break down technically
reasoning: Scutt notes that US real yields at 239 basis points are approaching the highs seen in 2023, and that Treasury note futures have broken out of a symmetrical triangle pattern to the downside. From a technical perspective, this points to a retest of the lows in 2023 when the 10-year yield topped 5%. He also cites the large amount of debt issuance, including from hyperscalers and Treasury front-loading, as fundamental pressure on yields. The combination of higher nominal and real yields creates a very tough backdrop for risk assets.
quote: So this is looking here. This is the real yield for ten years. So 239 basis points. You can see it's getting really close to those levels in 2023. When you look at some of the patterns in Treasury note futures at the moment we have a symmetrical triangle and it's broken out from underneath that at the moment. From a pure technicians perspective, that points to a retest of the lows we saw back in in 2023, and that was when we topped 5% for that ten year note yield. So it's conceivable that we're going to get there. And then you look at the amount of debt issuance that's out there as well.

headline: David Scutt argues gold has lost its safe-haven characteristics and has become a momentum trade, with higher real yields and a stronger USD toxic for the metal
reasoning: Scutt observes that gold's behaviour has changed and it is no longer acting as a safe haven. He notes a pattern of momentum traders rotating between asset classes — from crypto into precious metals and then into the AI space — suggesting the same cohort drives these moves. Central bank purchases remain a structural positive but are not the dominant driver currently. He identifies higher real yields and a stronger US dollar as particularly toxic headwinds for gold in the current environment.
quote: Gold's characteristics for the moment have changed. So it's no longer a safe haven. Now. It could return. I probably suspect in time, it will return to being some sort of form of a safe haven. But when you look at what was going on in crypto, you had this big momentum swing, and then all of a sudden there was a big pullback. And then it was just at that moment that you saw gold, silver, other precious metals start to go in rally as well. There are other factors that are in play. Certainly central bank purchases over the years have been a constant positive, but I suspect it's become more of a momentum trade at the moment. So you have basically the same cohort of traders and investors switching from one asset class to the next, like crypto into precious metals. Then it's been the AI space more recently. So we'll see what happens in time. But certainly when you put higher real yields, higher US dollar into the to the mix when it comes to gold, that's absolutely toxic for gold.

headline: David Scutt sees a strengthening US dollar as an additional headwind for risk assets and non-yielding assets like gold and crypto
reasoning: Scutt points to the DXY breaking out again technically, driven by higher nominal and real yields alongside rising risk aversion. So you look at those assets that don't offer a yield of very low yield and they struggle. So gold look at what's going on in cryptocurrencies. Yes you've seen the bouncing around but they've been very depressed. This is the US dollar index. Just the simple DXY. You can see here just from a technical perspective we've broken out again that's been on the back of nominal yields pushing higher real yields pushing higher risk aversion.

headline: David Scutt sees iron ore price action driven more by technical factors than fundamentals, with rising energy costs adding to input cost pressures

I think it's got a lot more to do with technical factors than it does to have anything to do with, uh, any sort of fundamentals you hear, like now that talks about port strikes. Then there was like no positive about you going to going to have the ability for, uh, weather patterns to go mean that it would be easier for shipping to go and take place. This is all headlines over the past week or so, but when I looked at the other chart, it was threatening to go and break to fresh lows earlier this week. And then lo and behold, technical support boom! It went straight back higher again. So, uh, when it comes to a fundamental basis though, iron ore to go and ship it need to go and have energy. Energy prices go up. It means you've got to go and pay higher input costs. That means the end customer is like you have to pay more as well.

headline: David Scutt sees rising probability of an RBA rate hike in August following strong jobs data, though remains personally cautious on the need to move
reasoning: Scutt notes the market has repriced the probability of an August RBA hike to around 41% following strong employment data, up from around 20% for most of the prior month. He has been staunch in his view that the RBA does not yet need to hike and can wait to see the transmission of price increases. However, he acknowledges that rising energy prices and the return of the full petrol excise create an inflationary environment, and that persistent inflation risks becoming entrenched in wage expectations. He admits his personal call is increasingly at odds with market pricing.
quote: I've been staunch. I think that there's no great need for the RBA to go and hike yet. They can still wait to go and see the transmission mechanism of those price hikes coming through. But I've got to admit that in an environment where you've got energy prices going higher, you've got the excise on petrol coming back into full effect as well. That's going to be an inflationary environment. And the longer that inflation remains in the system, the more it becomes entrenched in the way that people think about their wage demands and things like that. So I've got to admit that whilst I think that the RBA is done, certainly at this point in time, the rest of my call are moving in the other direction.

headline: David Scutt flags Fed rate hike risk is rising with nearly 60bp of hikes now priced into the curve through June next year

The US economy has continued to chug along despite headwinds, and inflation pressures from energy prices and geopolitical tensions in the Gulf region add to the concern.

Big turnaround from what you saw at the start of March. We had multiple cuts priced in over the same period. Uh, the inflation problem. The fed is making a lot of noise about the need to go and tackle inflation. You put that into the mix. It's hard to argue that those shifts are not that those risks are not tilting towards the fed having to act and act pretty soon.

headline: Stonex's David Scott warns rising yields and stronger USD create headwinds for precious metals, crypto and speculative AI-linked tech stocks
reasoning: Scott explains that assets priced in US dollars with little or no yield — such as precious metals, crypto, and highly speculative AI-build-up tech stocks — face headwinds when real and nominal yields are rising and the dollar is strengthening. So you put that into the mix. Those two factors alone, I think, go a long way to explaining why the market cannot go and get a turnaround in sentiment at this point in time. And so to me, the more broad aspect is that until that dynamic changes, you're going to have this sell and rallies environment continue.

headline: Stonex's David Scott identifies bearish technical signals in Korea's KOSPI and the SOX index as leading indicators for the broader AI trade downturn

On the left-hand side, you've got the Cospy futures and the red arrow that I'm pointing to there, that weekly candle, that's known as dark cloud cover. And it's not a really well-known technical signal, but it suggests that moment there was downside risk emerging in that particular market, which I think is leading the broader AI move at this point in time. So you can see since that weekly candle, it's just been one-way traffic and there is the potential for an extension of that move further. Then you look at the socks index on the right-hand side, and you've got a blue candle there. And that on the weekly chart was a bearish key reversal candle. I'm not going to be rushing in to go and buying it deep at this point in time, but I am watching the price action really closely, particularly on the weekly timeframe to get a sense as to where directional shifts may lie over longer timeframes.

headline: Stonex's David Scott sees US 10-year Treasury yields at risk of new highs, reinforcing bearish risk sentiment

So 10-year yields, we take the actual underlying bond. This is the futures contract for that. So basically, it gives you a steer as to where you see directional risk for yields coming at the moment. And what we've seen over recent months is just being this relentless grinding move higher. And you've got these technical patterns called rising wedges, which are what's called a bearish continuation pattern, which basically means it keeps going lower over time. And what that's telling me at this point in time is that despite all the talk about the soft inflation prints last week, the price action is really not confirming that. It suggests that the lows that we saw that were set back in June are at risk.

headline: Stonex's David Scott sees US dollar in consolidation with upward bias, driven by rising real and nominal yields

headline: Stonex's David Scott highlights Brent crude approaching $90/barrel as an inflationary risk and RBA policy complication

That's going to heat pressure on the RBA to continue lifting rates, despite what are some pretty obvious catalysts out there that suggest that maybe downside risks are starting to emerge when it comes to economic activity and with it eventually inflation.

headline: Stonex's David Scott sees directional risk skewing toward a softer US dollar as Fed hawkishness narrative fades

And that's one thing that has been a really big factor that we're seeing over the course of recent weeks is that real yields. So once you're going to strip out the inflation component of those normal yields remain very, very elevated compared to historic norms. And at levels that we've seen a lot of problems emerge in the past or riskier assets.

headline: Stonex's David Scott flags risk of AI sentiment unwind after Meta's data centre spare capacity announcement signals oversupply concerns

You've got one of the hyperscalers saying, well, we've actually got spare capacity available. So to me, when I look at that, I still don't think that the market has fully appreciated the risk that, hey, maybe we've gone and put the cut before the horse and run a little bit too hard before we actually see the revenue gross coming through in these big companies.
